entries.name: Irreecha (traditional thanksgiving)
entries.capsule: Oromo thanksgiving at the end of the rainy season, marked with prayer for peace at water; Minnesota organizers set their own dates.
entries.dateRule: A traditional date at the end of the rainy season, usually September or October. A religious leader traditionally announces it by watching the sky and lunar calendar, Teferi Tafa told Ampers. Minnesota dates are set by organizers and are listed as separate entries.
entries.whatItMarks: Thanks to Waaqa for past blessings, prayer for peace and reconciliation, and the end of the rains and start of the Birraa harvest season. Ethiopia banned it for over a century, MNopedia says, and many remember the 2016 deaths at the Arsadi gathering.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: Families gather at a Twin Cities park or lake in cultural clothing to pray, sing, dance and share food such as badenna. MNopedia names Lake Nokomis each September; for 2026, the organizer's listing and Oromo Diaspora Media name Powderhorn Park, while one lone report says Lake Nokomis. OPride reported an Oct. 3, 2009 celebration at Lake Nokomis. Attendance figures were not found.

entries.name: Irreechaa Malkaa at Powderhorn Park
entries.capsule: Minnesota Irreecha by the water at Powderhorn Park, listed by Oromo Irreecha Minnesota for September 19, 2026.
entries.dateRule: Set each year by Oromo Irreecha Minnesota. Later years have not been announced.

dates.source: Oromo Irreecha Minnesota, irreechaa.org; Oromo Diaspora Media

entries.name: Irreecha at Lake Nokomis (Hawaasa Oromoo Minnesota)
entries.capsule: One lone report places an Irreecha at Lake Nokomis on September 19, 2026; other sources name Powderhorn Park, so this is unconfirmed.
entries.dateRule: As reported for 2026 by one write-up only. It conflicts with sources placing the day's event at Powderhorn Park, and no organizer notice was found, so the date is not treated as confirmed. It may be a second gathering or a mistaken place.

dates.source: One lone report on an Australian advocacy website; it conflicts with sources placing the event at Powderhorn Park

entries.whatItMarks: Irreecha, the Oromo thanksgiving, with remembrance of those killed at Arsadi in 2016.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: The one write-up describes prayers, performances, traditional attire, elders, youth and children, and names no speakers or attendance. Because it conflicts with sources naming Powderhorn Park, it should not be read as confirmed.

entries.name: Irreechaa Tulluu
entries.capsule: Spring Irreecha, traditionally on a mountaintop, marking the end of the dry season; held at Powderhorn Park on May 2, 2026.
entries.dateRule: Set each year by the Irreechaa Organization in Minnesota, in May. Later years have not been announced.
entries.whatItMarks: The end of the dry season, with prayers for summer rain, peace and good harvests.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: Held at Powderhorn Park on May 2, 2026. Ampers also reports May gatherings at a selected Twin Cities park.

entries.name: Oromo Week and the OSFNA tournament
alsoKnownAs: Oromo Sports Federation in North America tournament
entries.capsule: A week of Oromo soccer, music and family gathering; St. Paul hosted August 1 to 8, 2026, marking 30 years.
entries.dateRule: Annual summer tournament that rotates among North American cities. Check the federation each year; a Minnesota date is not guaranteed.

dates.source: Oromo Community of Georgia listing; Allianz Field for the Aug. 8 final

entries.whatItMarks: A gathering of Oromo clubs and families. The federation dates its first tournament to Toronto in 1996.
entries.howCelebratedInMinnesota: For 2026, listings show a festival at Central High School in St. Paul, nightly matches and a final at Allianz Field on August 8. MNopedia says St. Paul first hosted in 2011 and both cities' mayors declared Oromo Week.
